title: The Arena at Dawn
story:
When the night at last ended and the sun rose up out of the waters, Kamsa gave his order: let the wrestling begin.

He had spent the dark hours with his omens and his dreams, turning them over and over the way a man turns a key in a lock that will not open. But morning came, and with it he set about turning his dread into a plan. The wrestling festival was to be the great public show of his reign, the day when all of Mathura gathered to watch the king's wrestlers prove their strength. Now it would serve a second purpose, one he kept to himself behind his steady face, and he gave the word for everything to be made ready, sending it out through the palace and into the streets, and the city answered.

All through the city the arena was made ready. Men went to work on the wrestling ground, smoothing the earth and raising the banners, and the drums and kettledrums began to sound, the noise rolling out over the houses until there was no corner of Mathura that did not know the festival had begun. Ropes were drawn around the wrestling ground, and the morning sun climbed slowly over the stands. The sound was meant to be joyful, and it was, in the bright early air — and yet it carried an edge to anyone who knew the king and what his festivals had come to mean.

The people came. Citizens and country folk poured in, brahmins and kshatriyas at their head, and took their places around the arena until the stands were full and the ground was ringed with faces, the whole city turned out in its best. They came in great numbers, and the sound of them was a low, expectant murmur that rose and fell like the sea. Kamsa himself climbed to the royal dais, his ministers around him, and sat looking out over the crowd he had gathered — the crowd that would watch whatever he had arranged for them to watch, and cheer at whatever he told them was worth cheering.

The wrestlers entered and took their places: Chanura and Mushtika, the strongest of the king's fighters, and with them Kuta, Shala, and Toshala — each of them practiced and dangerous, each of them waiting for the signal to fight, their oiled bodies shining in the morning light. They moved through the arena with the easy confidence of men who had never been beaten, and the crowd murmured its approval as they passed.

And then, summoned by the Bhoja king, the cowherds arrived — Nanda at their head, with the other men of Vrindavan, come to the city as guests bearing their offerings. They were country men in a king's city, and they looked it, and yet they carried themselves with the quiet dignity of invited guests. They moved through the crowd with the awkward politeness of people far from home, their gifts held before them. There were greetings and gifts, and the festival settled into its appointed order, and no one yet spoke of what it was really for.

The stage was set. The drums beat on. And Kamsa, at the center of it all, watched the gate.
reflection: The passage moves from the intimacy of Kamsa's fear to the great public theater of the arena — a king turning private dread into spectacle. Everything here is told in the language of preparation and display, and the effect is ominous: every drum and banner is being readied for a confrontation no one will announce.
next_story_tease: But the brothers had not yet reached the arena, and between them and its gate stood a creature no wrestler could match.
hero_scene: The wrestling arena at dawn, drums sounding and banners flying, with Kamsa seated on the royal dais as the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika take their places and Nanda's cowherds arrive bearing offerings.
